claim: Terpenoids constitute the largest class of natural products made by living organisms with over 80,000 structures identified.
source: With over 80,000 structures identified, terpenoids constitute the largest class of natural products made by living organisms (Christianson, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Christianson, 2017.

claim: Most terpenoid natural products are known from plants.
source: Most terpenoid natural products are known from plants (Chen et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Bacteria are rich sources of terpenoid natural products.
source: bacteria (Yamada et al., 2015; Dickschat, 2016) and fungi (Keller et al., 2005; Schmidt-Dannert, 2015) are also rich sources.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yamada et al., 2015 and Dickschat, 2016.

claim: Fungi are rich sources of terpenoid natural products.
source: bacteria (Yamada et al., 2015; Dickschat, 2016) and fungi (Keller et al., 2005; Schmidt-Dannert, 2015) are also rich sources.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Keller et al., 2005 and Schmidt-Dannert, 2015.

claim: Dictyostelid social amoebae have the genetic capacity to produce monoterpenes (C10), sesquiterpenes (C15) and diterpenes (C20).
source: Recently we have shown that dictyostelid social amoebae, a class of eukaryotic soil microorganisms, also have the genetic capacity to produce monoterpenes (C10), sesquiterpenes (C15) and diterpenes (C20) (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Dictyostelid social amoebae have a unique life cycle consisting of both unicellular and multicellular phases.
source: Dictyostelid social amoebae have a unique life cycle, consisting of both unicellular and multicellular phases.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about dictyostelid social amoebae.

claim: When bacterial food supply becomes scarce, dictyostelid amoebae start to aggregate and go through morphological changes to form fruiting bodies.
source: When their bacterial food supply becomes scarce, amoebae start to aggregate, going through clearly-defined morphological changes to eventually form fruiting bodies (Kessin, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kessin, 2001.

claim: The multicellular stages of D. discoideum life cycle are characterized by the emission of a complex mixture of volatile organic compounds dominated by sesquiterpenes.
source: Our recent studies illustrated that the multicellular stages of the life cycle of both D. discoideum (Chen et al., 2016) and D. purpureum (Chen et al., 2018) are characterized by the emission of a complex mixture of volatile organic compounds that is dominated by sesquiterpenes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Chen et al., 2018.

claim: The multicellular stages of D. purpureum life cycle are characterized by the emission of a complex mixture of volatile organic compounds dominated by sesquiterpenes.
source: Our recent studies illustrated that the multicellular stages of the life cycle of both D. discoideum (Chen et al., 2016) and D. purpureum (Chen et al., 2018) are characterized by the emission of a complex mixture of volatile organic compounds that is dominated by sesquiterpenes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Chen et al., 2018.

claim: Most terpenoids produced by D. discoideum and D. purpureum appear to be species-specific.
source: While some terpenoids are produced by both species, most appear to be species-specific (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: The biological function of terpenoids produced by D. discoideum and D. purpureum is completely unknown.
source: The biological function of these terpenoids is completely unknown.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the lack of knowledge at the time of writing.

claim: The D. discoideum genome contains nine full-length genes (DdTPS1-9) encoding terpene synthases.
source: The D. discoideum genome contains nine full-length genes (DdTPS1-9) encoding terpene synthases, the pivotal enzymes that create the terpenoid carbon skeleton (Christianson, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic data and a citation to Christianson, 2017.

claim: All nine DdTPS genes are expressed during the multicellular stage of D. discoideum.
source: All nine genes are expressed during the multicellular stage, suggesting a role for volatile terpenoid biosynthesis in fruiting body development.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data.

claim: Biochemical characterization of DdTPS1-9 revealed terpene synthase activity for all tested enzymes.
source: Indeed, biochemical characterization of the encoded proteins DdTPS1-9 revealed terpene synthase activity for all tested enzymes.
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical assay data.

claim: The sesquiterpene products of DdTPS1-4, DdTPS6, DdTPS7 and DdTPS9 could be detected in the volatile bouquet of D. discoideum during multicellular development.
source: The sesquiterpene products of DdTPS1-4, DdTPS6, DdTPS7 and DdTPS9, as well as the diterpene product of DdTPS5, could be detected in the volatile bouquet of D. discoideum during multicellular development (Chen et al., 2016; Rabe et al., 2016a; Rinkel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016, Rabe et al., 2016a, and Rinkel et al., 2017.

claim: The diterpene product of DdTPS5 could be detected in the volatile bouquet of D. discoideum during multicellular development.
source: The sesquiterpene products of DdTPS1-4, DdTPS6, DdTPS7 and DdTPS9, as well as the diterpene product of DdTPS5, could be detected in the volatile bouquet of D. discoideum during multicellular development (Chen et al., 2016; Rabe et al., 2016a; Rinkel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016, Rabe et al., 2016a, and Rinkel et al., 2017.

claim: D. discoideum releases the monoterpene linalool that is produced by several recombinant terpene synthases including DdTPS2, DdTPS3 and DdTPS9.
source: D. discoideum also released the monoterpene linalool that was produced by several recombinant terpene synthases including DdTPS2, DdTPS3 and DdTPS9, suggesting that at least one of these enzymes functions as a monoterpene synthase in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on volatile emissions and enzyme assays.

claim: The in vitro products of all DdTPSs except DdTPS8 could be detected in the volatile bouquet of D. discoideum.
source: In brief, the in vitro products of all DdTPSs except DdTPS8 could be detected in the volatile bouquet of D. discoideum.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of in vitro enzyme assays and volatile profiling data.

claim: DdTPS8 has sesquiterpene synthase activity but does not produce mono- or diterpenes in vitro.
source: DdTPS8 has sesquiterpene synthase activity, but does not produce mono- or diterpenes in vitro (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: DdTPS8 exhibits the second highest level of expression among all nine DdTPS genes during development.
source: DdTPS8 exhibits the second highest level of expression among all nine DdTPS genes during development
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data.

claim: The major sesquiterpene product of DdTPS8 was not detected in the D. discoideum volatiles.
source: so it was surprising to see that the major sesquiterpene product of DdTPS8 was not detected in the D. discoideum volatiles (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: CYPs are heme-containing proteins that catalyze a wide variety of oxidative reactions.
source: CYPs are heme-containing proteins that catalyze a wide variety of oxidative reactions (Coon, 2005), often on terpenoid substrates (Hamberger and Bak, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coon, 2005.

claim: CYPs often catalyze oxidative reactions on terpenoid substrates.
source: CYPs are heme-containing proteins that catalyze a wide variety of oxidative reactions (Coon, 2005), often on terpenoid substrates (Hamberger and Bak, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hamberger and Bak, 2013.

claim: DdTPS8 and CYP521A1 are physically clustered on chromosome six.
source: Here we present conclusive evidence that the DdTPS8 sesquiterpene product is modified by a CYP that is physically clustered with DdTPS8 on chromosome six and produces a novel trisnorsesquiterpene named as discodiene.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic location data.

claim: CYP521A1 modifies the DdTPS8 sesquiterpene product to produce a novel trisnorsesquiterpene named discodiene.
source: Here we present conclusive evidence that the DdTPS8 sesquiterpene product is modified by a CYP that is physically clustered with DdTPS8 on chromosome six and produces a novel trisnorsesquiterpene named as discodiene.
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A DdTPS8-knockout mutant of D. discoideum failed to produce discodiene.
source: A DdTPS8-knockout mutant of D. discoideum, which failed to produce discodiene, showed slower progression in development than the wild type strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical profiling data of the mutant.

claim: A DdTPS8-knockout mutant of D. discoideum showed slower progression in development than the wild type strain.
source: A DdTPS8-knockout mutant of D. discoideum, which failed to produce discodiene, showed slower progression in development than the wild type strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental phenotype data.

claim: DdTPS8 catalyzes the formation of a sesquiterpene alcohol as a single product when incubated with farnesyl diphosphate (FDP).
source: After protein purification by Ni2+-NTA affinity chromatography, the recombinant DdTPS8 enzyme was incubated with its substrate farnesyl diphosphate (FDP), resulting in the formation of a sesquiterpene alcohol as a single product.
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme assay data.

claim: The product of DdTPS8 is a new bicyclic sesquiterpenoid named discoidol.
source: The compound was purified and structure elucidation by NMR spectroscopy (Supplementary file 1) revealed a new bicyclic sesquiterpenoid, which was named discoidol (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: Discoidol is a stereoisomer of the known sesquiterpene alcohol jinkoh-eremol.
source: Discoidol is a stereoisomer of the known sesquiterpene alcohol jinkoh-eremol (Nakanishi et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison and a citation to Nakanishi et al., 1983.

claim: The absolute configuration of discoidol is (4S,5S,7S).
source: These experiments resulted in the assigned absolute configuration of (4S,5S,7S)-discoidol.
evidence: The claim is supported by isotopic labeling experiments and NMR spectroscopy.

claim: The cyclization mechanism of discoidol synthase starts with a 1,10-cyclization of FDP with attack of water to yield hedycaryol.
source: The proposed cyclization mechanism of discoidol synthase (Figure 1D) starts with a 1,10-cyclization of FDP with attack of water to yield the neutral intermediate hedycaryol.
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanistic analysis and isotopic labeling experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The DdTPS8 mutant lacks a major peak (peak one) whose structure was unknown and has a molecular mass of 162.
source: In comparison to the wild type, the DdTPS8 mutant lacked a major peak (peak one in Figure 2B) whose structure was unknown. This unknown compound appeared to have a molecular mass of 162
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The unknown compound with molecular mass 162 is consistent with a degraded sesquiterpene that had lost a fragment containing three carbon atoms and one oxygen atom.
source: This unknown compound appeared to have a molecular mass of 162, consistent with the mass of a degraded sesquiterpene that had lost a fragment containing three carbon atoms and one oxygen atom.
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data and inference about molecular composition.

claim: Analysis of the D. discoideum genome led to the identification of a total of 54 putative CYP genes.
source: Analysis of the D. discoideum genome led to the identification of a total of 54 putative CYP genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: Among the 54 putative CYP genes in D. discoideum, 41 were annotated as full-length intact genes.
source: Among them, 41 were annotated as full-length intact genes whereas the rest were pseudogenes or partial genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic annotation data.

claim: The 41 full-length CYP genes in D. discoideum were assigned to 17 families and 34 subfamilies.
source: The 41 full-length genes were assigned to 17 families and 34 subfamilies (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic classification data.

claim: Three CYP genes showed significant correlation coefficients with DdTPS8 with a P value lower than 0.001: CYP521A1 (r = 0.994), CYP508C1 (r = 0.992) and CYP519C1 (r = 0.951).
source: Among the 41 CYP genes, three showed significant correlation coefficients with DdTPS8 exhibiting a P value lower than 0.001 (Supplementary file 3): CYP521A1 (r = 0.994), CYP508C1 (r = 0.992) and CYP519C1 (r = 0.951).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: CYP521A1, CYP508C1, and CYP519C1 showed maximal level of expression at 16 hr during multicellular development, like DdTPS8.
source: These three CYP genes, like DdTPS8, showed a maximal level of expression at 16 hr during multicellular development (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CYP521A1 is located 685 bp away from DdTPS8 in a head-to-head configuration on chromosome 6.
source: We also noticed that the top candidate CYP521A1 is located 685 bp away from DdTPS8 in a head-to-head configuration on chromosome 6 (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic location data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: E. coli cells harboring DdTPS8, redB, and CYP521A1 produced both discoidol and the unknown terpenoid with a molecular mass of m/z = 162.
source: Indeed, GC-MS analysis confirmed the formation of both discoidol with a molecular mass of m/z = 222 (Figure 4B) and the unknown terpenoid with a molecular mass of m/z = 162 (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: E. coli cells harboring DdTPS8, redB, and CYP508C1 produced only discoidol and no further terpenoids.
source: E. coli cells harboring DdTPS8, redB, and CYP508C1, another P450 gene highly coexpressed with DdTPS8, produced only discoidol and no further terpenoids (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When CYP521A1 and redB were expressed in the absence of DdTPS8, no terpene formation was observed.
source: When CYP521A1 and redB were expressed in the absence of DdTPS8, no terpene formation was observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by enzyme assay data.

claim: The molecular ion at m/z = 162 in the EI mass spectrum points to a degradation of discoidol with loss of a fragment representing a molecular weight of 60 Da.
source: However, the molecular ion at m/z = 162 in the EI mass spectrum (Figure 5A), pointed to a degradation of discoidol with loss of a fragment representing a molecular weight of 60 Da.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The degradation product of discoidol is a trisnorsesquiterpene with incorporation of twelve 13C atoms.
source: The same reaction with completely labeled (13C15)discoidol, obtained from (13C15)FDP (Rabe et al., 2015) with discoidol synthase, produced a degradation product with incorporation of twelve 13C atoms (Figure 5B), demonstrating that the degradation product is a trisnorsesquiterpene.
evidence: The claim is supported by isotopic labeling experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The tentatively identified compound produced by CYP521A1 from discoidol is a new natural product named discodiene.
source: The tentatively identified compound is a new natural product for which we propose the name discodiene.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis and isotopic labeling experiments.

claim: At 16 hr of starvation, the multicellular development of the DdTPS8 mutant was delayed compared to the wild type.
source: However, a difference was observed after 16 hr of starvation: the multicellular development of the mutant was delayed compared to the wild type (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental phenotype data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At 16 hr, the wild type D. discoideum cells formed fingers, whereas the DdTPS8 mutant was mainly at the tipped aggregate stage.
source: At this time point, the wild type cells formed fingers, whereas the mutant was mainly at the tipped aggregate stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental phenotype observations.

claim: At 20 hr, the wild type D. discoideum began to transition from fingers into Mexican hats, while the DdTPS8 mutant was delayed at the finger stage.
source: At 20 hr (Figure 6), the wild type began to transition from fingers into so-called 'Mexican hats', so a mix of the two stages was observed, while the mutant was delayed at the finger stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental phenotype data shown in Figure 6.

claim: At 24 hr, the wild type D. discoideum began entering the culmination stage, while the DdTPS8 mutant was still mostly at the finger stage with some Mexican hats visible.
source: At 24 hr, the wild type began entering the culmination stage, which involves complex cell movements to form a ball of spores carried on top of a cellular stalk. However, the mutant was still mostly at the finger stage with some Mexican hats visible (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental phenotype data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Eventually, both the wild type and the DdTPS8 mutant developed into well-proportioned fruiting bodies with stalks and spores that were largely indistinguishable.
source: Eventually, both the wild type and the mutant developed into well-proportioned fruiting bodies, with stalks and spores, and they were largely indistinguishable (Figure 6, 54h).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental phenotype data shown in Figure 6.

claim: No differences in spore formation and germination were observed between the wild type and the DdTPS8 mutant.
source: Spore formation and germination were also compared but no differences were observed between the wild type and the DdTPS8 mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: DdTPS8 has a function during later stages of multicellular development in D. discoideum, during the transition from fingers to Mexican hats.
source: These data suggest that DdTPS8 has a function during later stages of multicellular development in D. discoideum, during the transition from fingers to Mexican hats, which is consistent with its temporal expression pattern (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the developmental phenotype data and gene expression pattern.

claim: Two additional putative TPS-CYP gene clusters were identified in D. discoideum: DdTPS2-CYP519C1 and DdTPS3-CYP515A1.
source: Following the functional validation of the DdTPS8-CYP521A1 gene cluster, we examined other members of the TPS and CYP families in D. discoideum and identified two additional putative TPS-CYP gene clusters (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: DdTPS2 is organized in a head-to-head fashion with CYP519C1 and the two are separated by an intergenic region of 580 bp.
source: DdTPS2 is organized in a head-to-head fashion with CYP519C1 and the two are separated by an intergenic region of 580 bp.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic location data.

claim: A total of 54 putative CYP genes were found in D. purpureum.
source: We found a total of 54 putative CYP genes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: Among the 54 putative CYP genes in D. purpureum, 47 were annotated as full-length intact genes.
source: Among them, 47 were annotated as full-length intact genes whereas the remaining are partial genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic annotation data.

claim: The 47 full-length CYP genes in D. purpureum were assigned to 12 families and 29 subfamilies.
source: The 47 full-length genes were assigned to 12 families and 29 subfamilies.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic classification data.

claim: Two putative TPS-CYP clusters were identified in D. purpureum: DpTPS5-CYP5121A1_Dp and DdTPS12-CYP919E1_Dp.
source: By examining the physical locations of TPS and CYP genes, two putative TPS-CYP clusters were identified in D. purpureum: DpTPS5 is linked to CYP5121A1_Dp with an intergenic region of 612 bp and DdTPS12 is linked to CYP919E1_Dp with an intergenic region of 900 bp (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: DdTPS8 is a microbial terpene synthase that shares many mechanistic features of typical plant terpene synthases.
source: DdTPS8 is a microbial terpene synthase that shares many mechanistic features of other typical plant terpene synthases, such as a protonation-induced cyclization of a neutral intermediate, a 1,2-hydride shift and a methyl group migration (Degenhardt et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanistic analysis and a citation to Degenhardt et al., 2009.

claim: The most closely related terpene synthase to DdTPS8 in D. discoideum is DdTPS4, which forms the acyclic sesquiterpene alcohol (E)-nerolidol.
source: It is interesting to note that the most closely related terpene synthase in D. discoideum, DdTPS4, also forms a sesquiterpene alcohol (Chen et al., 2016). However, the product of DdTPS4, (E)-nerolidol, is an acyclic compound in contrast to the cyclic product of DdTPS8.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and a citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Jinkoh-eremol has been previously isolated from agarwood (Aquilaria sp.), a eudicotyledon flowering plant.
source: It is also interesting to note that a stereoisomer of discoidol known as jinkoh-eremol has been previously isolated from an agarwood (Aquilaria sp.), a eudicotyledon flowering plant (Nakanishi et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakanishi et al., 1983.

claim: Convergent evolution has occurred in D. discoideum and plants for the biosynthesis of similar terpenes.
source: Since the biosynthesis of jinkoh-eremol in agarwood is most likely catalyzed by typical plant terpene synthases, which are only distantly related to the microbial type terpene synthases that include D. discoideum TPSs (Jia et al., 2016), convergent evolution has occurred in D. discoideum and plants for the biosynthesis of similar terpenes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from phylogenetic relationships and structural similarities, supported by a citation to Jia et al., 2016.

claim: Geosmin is a particularly widespread trisnorsesquiterpene compound in soil microorganisms that exhibits the smell of earth.
source: Another important member of this group is geosmin, a particularly widespread compound in soil microorganisms that exhibits the smell of earth.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about geosmin.

claim: A bifunctional terpene synthase catalyzes the formation of geosmin involving initial cyclization to an enantiomer of hedycaryol followed by a second cyclization and oxidative cleavage of a 1-hydroxy-1-methylethyl unit.
source: it became later evident from feeding experiments (Dickschat et al., 2005) and characterization of the enzyme (Jiang et al., 2007) that a bifunctional terpene synthase catalyzes the formation of this compound involving initial cyclization to an enantiomer of hedycaryol followed by a second cyclization and oxidative cleavage of a 1-hydroxy-1-methylethyl unit.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dickschat et al., 2005 and Jiang et al., 2007.

claim: Oxidative dealkylations such as the reaction catalyzed by CYP521A1 are known from a few other cytochrome P450s, including angelicin synthase (CYP71AJ4) from Ammi majus.
source: Oxidative dealkylations such as the reaction catalyzed by CYP521A1 converting discoidol into discodiene are known from a few other cytochrome P450s, including angelicin synthase (CYP71AJ4) from Ammi majus (Larbat et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Larbat et al., 2009.

claim: Secologanin synthase (CYP72A1) from Catharanthus roseus catalyzes oxidative dealkylation reactions.
source: secologanin synthase (CYP72A1) from Catharanthus roseus (Irmler et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Irmler et al., 2000.

claim: DMNT/TMTT synthase (CYP82G1) from Arabidopsis catalyzes oxidative dealkylation reactions.
source: DMNT/TMTT synthase (CYP82G1) from Arabidopsis (Lee et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2010.

claim: Psoralene synthase catalyzes the degradation of (+)-marmesin to psoralene.
source: the degradation of (+)-marmesin to psoralene by the psoralene synthase (Stanjek et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stanjek et al., 1999.

claim: The culmination stage of D. discoideum development occurs at the end of development, between 16 and 24 hr after the process begins.
source: The culmination stage, which is marked by the onset of stalk formation, occurs at the end of development, between 16 and 24 hr after the process begins.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about D. discoideum development.

claim: A number of metabolites have been demonstrated to regulate Dictyostelium development, such as the polyketides DIF-1 and 4-methyl-5-pentylbenzene-1,3-diol.
source: A number of metabolites have been demonstrated to regulate Dictyostelium development, such as the polyketides DIF-1 (Thompson and Kay, 2000) and 4-methyl-5-pentylbenzene-1,3-diol (Anjard et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thompson and Kay, 2000 and Anjard et al., 2011.

claim: Gamma-aminobutyric acid, the nucleotide cyclic diguanylate, the cytokinin discadenine and an unidentified steroid regulate Dictyostelium development.
source: gamma-aminobutyric acid, the nucleotide cyclic diguanylate, the cytokinin discadenine and an unidentified steroid (Loomis, 2014; Schaap, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Loomis, 2014 and Schaap, 2016.

claim: Discodiene is a volatile compound.
source: One major difference between discodiene and these metabolites is that discodiene is a volatile.
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical properties of discodiene.

claim: Disrupting DdTPS8 did not fully block the development of D. discoideum.
source: Since disrupting DdTPS8 did not fully block the development of D. discoideum, discodiene might be merely a component of the volatile bouquet needed for development.
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental phenotype data.

claim: The organization of terpene synthase genes and CYP genes involved in the same biochemical pathway as metabolic gene clusters has been documented in bacteria.
source: The organization of terpenes synthase genes and CYP genes involved in the same biochemical pathway as metabolic gene clusters has been documented in a growing number of cases including bacteria (Nett et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nett et al., 2017.

claim: The organization of terpene synthase genes and CYP genes involved in the same biochemical pathway as metabolic gene clusters has been documented in fungi.
source: fungi (Quin et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Quin et al., 2014.

claim: The organization of terpene synthase genes and CYP genes involved in the same biochemical pathway as metabolic gene clusters has been documented in plants.
source: plants (Boutanaev et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boutanaev et al., 2015.

claim: The ortholog of DdTPS8 in D. purpureum is DpTPS6.
source: The ortholog of DdTPS8 in D. purpureum is DpTPS6 (Chen et al., 2018), which is not clustered with any CYP gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: D. purpureum lacks an ortholog of CYP521A1.
source: Moreover, D. purpureum lacks an ortholog of CYP521A1, implying that the D. purpureum may not produce discodiene
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: D. purpureum may not produce discodiene.
source: Moreover, D. purpureum lacks an ortholog of CYP521A1, implying that the D. purpureum may not produce discodiene, consist with the volatile profiling of this species (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of CYP521A1 ortholog and supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: DdTPS3-CYP515A1 and DpTPS5-CYP515A1_Dp are an orthologous pair.
source: In contrast, DdTPS3-CYP515A1 and DpTPS5-CYP515A1_Dp are an orthologous pair based on the orthology of the respective TPS genes (DdTPS3 and DpTPS5) (Chen et al., 2018) and CYP genes (CYP515A1 and CYP515A1-Dp are in the same subfamily).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claim: The D. discoideum genome contains 40 PKS genes.
source: The D. discoideum genome contains 40 PKS genes (Zucko et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zucko et al., 2007.

claim: The DdTPS8 mutant was obtained from the gridded collection of the Genome Wide Dictyostelium Insertion (GWDI) Project.
source: The DdTPS8 mutant was obtained from the gridded collection of the Genome Wide Dictyostelium Insertion (GWDI) Project (https://remi-seq.org).
evidence: The claim describes the source of the mutant strain.

claim: The DdTPS8 gene was disrupted by an insertion of a blasticidin resistance cassette between nucleotides 544 and 545 of the DdTPS8 open reading frame.
source: Therefore, we analyzed a D. discoideum mutant in which DdTPS8 was disrupted by an insertion of a blasticidin resistance cassette between nucleotides 544 and 545 of the DdTPS8 open reading frame (Figure 2A), which was verified by sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
